newsitem.title: UK: Oil swaps tussle clouds value of benchmark Brent.
newsitem.headline: Oil swaps tussle clouds value of benchmark Brent.

text.p: A tussle between two big trading houses designed to benefit opposing derivatives positions is obscuring the value of physical Brent crude, the price marker for much of the world oil market, traders said on Monday.

Wall Street refiner Phibro, a unit of Salomon Brothers Inc, and independent Swiss-based trader Glencore are trying to influence the reference price to return profits on Brent swaps positions, or contracts for difference (CFDs), they said.
Two Brent cargoes, due to load in the first four days of March, traded at prices 16 cents a barrel apart on Monday.
For a standard cargo of Brent, which usually loads 500,000 barrels, this represents a difference of nearly $80,000 in the price.
"This has nothing to do with the value of Dated (physical) Brent. We're in a week which is quite crucial for (Brent) CFD positions," said a North Sea crude trader.
Traders at Phibro and Glencore were unavailable for comment.
Leading market players said Phibro was aiming to depress the reference price to benefit a "short" swaps position while Glencore was keen to see it higher.
"To be honest, the market today is a joke," said a trader for a major oil company.

Crude swaps, or CFDs, are agreements to exchange fixed and floating price exposure on a nominal amount of oil over a set period of time. At the end of the agreed period, the swap buyer pays the seller the difference if prices drop below the agreed price and vice versa.
CFDs generally have a life of anything from a couple of days to a year. The shorter the term the more vulnerable the swap to manipulation, dealers said.
Glencore, the traders said, was prepared to pay over the odds for the physical oil it needs in order to inflate the Brent benchmark price used by the industry for settling swaps positions.
The assessments are often weighted to reflect reported trades of physical Brent cargoes due for delivery within a fortnight.

Last week Brent was reported to have traded at discounts of 19, 13 and two cents to March 15-day forward paper, in addition to Monday's deals at March Brent plus four cents and April Brent +32 cents, equivalent to March less 13 cents.
"You won't find any logic in what's going on with Dated Brent at the moment," said a trader.

The value of Brent Blend crude oil, which is loaded onto tankers at Sullom Voe in the Shetland Islands, is vital for world markets as it is used as the benchmark for the pricing of many other physical crudes.
As Brent cargoes are relatively thinly traded -- there are only 42 full cargoes due to load in March -- it is not difficult to influence the reference price.
Manipulation is a regular feature of oil markets, and while not illegal, if sustained can damage liquidity.
"Plenty of people are unwilling to get involved until this Brent game is sorted out," said a trader of the North Sea market on Monday.
